name: lh1_incremental_build
stressor: long-horizon multi-turn BUILD from scratch: 8 dependent turns incrementally grow a real expression-calculator library (tokenizer -> precedence/paren parser -> full operator set -> unary ops -> right-assoc power -> variables & assignment -> built-in functions -> uniform CalcError handling). setup() ships ONLY a README stating the end-goal plus an unimplemented stub; every line of working code is produced across the eight turns.
source_note: Hand-built greenfield project: calc.py, an infix arithmetic expression evaluator exposed as a Calculator class (.eval(line) returns a number or None for an assignment) plus a module-level evaluate(expr, env=None). setup() writes README.md (the full end-goal contract) and a calc.py stub whose Calculator.eval raises NotImplementedError, so NOTHING works until the agent builds it. Eight dependent turns: (1) tokenizer + integer/float literals + the four basic ops with correct +/- vs * // precedence, (2) parentheses + clear errors for unmatched parens, (3) the remaining operators // % **, (4) unary minus/plus, (5) right-associative ** that binds tighter than unary minus on its left but looser on its right (so -2**2 == -4 and 2**-1 == 0.5 and 2**3**2 == 512), (6) variables: bareword lookup + 'name = expr' assignment via .eval returning None and persisting in the Calculator across calls, (7) built-in call syntax abs/min/max/pow/sqrt with comma args and arity checks, (8) make every failure raise a single CalcError subclass with a useful message (unknown name, division by zero, unexpected/!trailing token, unmatched paren, unknown function, bad arity, empty input) and never a bare Python exception. stdlib only, no third-party deps, no network.
discriminator: This stresses PER-TURN COST FLATNESS under a long horizon. By turn 8 the whole working set is one ~150-line calc.py plus a fixed README contract; a bounded-slice agent re-reads exactly that file and the standing contract each turn, so its per-call input stays ~flat across all 8 turns. A growing-transcript agent must instead carry every prior turn's full edit/diff/tool-output history live, so its per-call input climbs turn over turn (and with it the dollar cost), even though the relevant context per turn is constant. Turns 5 and 8 are the trap: getting right-associativity/unary-precedence (turn 5) and uniform CalcError wrapping (turn 8) correct requires recalling the exact tokenizer/parser shape and error sites laid down in turns 1-4 and 6-7 -- a slice agent re-derives this from the current calc.py, while a transcript agent leans on increasingly distant turns and is likelier to regress an earlier operator or leak a raw ZeroDivisionError/KeyError.
